paragraphs: This paper studies how aggressively language-model weights can be compressed while preserving useful performance. It focuses on quantization-aware training, where training accounts for the restricted numerical values available after compression. The authors examine both the number of bits used per weight and the choice of quantization format, treating them as linked design decisions.

Their empirical study finds that weight quantization based on k-means performs better than integer formats in the low-bit settings examined. K-means uses clusters to choose representative weight values, making the available values responsive to the weights being compressed. The authors also report that this approach can be implemented efficiently on standard hardware.

The strongest result concerns a fixed inference memory budget: one-bit weights achieve the best performance on the generative downstream tasks studied. This makes the memory constraint central to interpreting the finding. By evaluating these tasks rather than relying only on perplexity, the paper connects compression choices more directly to what the resulting models can actually do.
icml-2026-1-bit-wonder-improving-qat-per.tldr: An empirical study finds that k-means quantization improves low-bit training, with one-bit weights performing best on tested generative tasks under a fixed inference memory budget.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a model’s explanation helps an observer predict how that model will behave on related inputs. This provides a positive test of explanations: they may communicate useful decision criteria even when other tests expose errors or inconsistencies. The authors introduce Normalized Simulatability Gain, or NSG, to measure this predictive contribution.

They evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight models using 7,000 counterfactual examples spanning health, business, and ethics. Self-explanations improve predictions of model behavior, with reported NSG values of 11–37%. They also provide more predictive information than explanations written by external models, including stronger ones. The authors interpret this advantage as evidence that models convey information about their own behavior that external explainers do not reproduce.

The results remain mixed at the level of individual explanations: across models, 5–15% are classified as egregiously misleading. The paper’s positive case is therefore specific. Self-explanations contain useful behavioral information, while their demonstrated predictive value coexists with serious failures that matter when using them for oversight.
icml-2026-a-positive-case-for-faithfulne.tldr: Self-explanations help predict LLM behavior better than external explanations in the reported evaluation, although a meaningful minority are seriously misleading.

paragraphs: Custom guardrails must enforce the particular rules of an application, including difficult cases near a policy boundary. The paper identifies a practical obstacle: generic safety models may miss these requirements, while training a dedicated classifier normally requires substantial labeled data. BARRED addresses the data problem using a task description and a small collection of unlabeled examples.

The framework breaks the domain into dimensions to generate examples with broad coverage. It then uses debate among agents to check labels, aiming to improve both the variety of examples and their agreement with the intended policy. These two stages address different requirements for training: encountering diverse situations and receiving trustworthy supervision for them.

Across the custom policies tested, small language models fine-tuned on BARRED data consistently outperform the proprietary LLMs and dedicated guardrail models used in the comparison. Ablation studies support the importance of both domain decomposition and debate. The findings suggest that carefully generated training data can make specialized guardrails accurate and efficient without extensive human annotation.
icml-2026-barred-synthetic-training-of-c.tldr: BARRED generates diverse, debate-checked training examples that let small models outperform tested alternatives on custom guardrail policies.

paragraphs: The paper considers a potential problem for AI evaluation: models may become capable enough that humans struggle to write discriminating questions, supply correct answers, or judge complete solutions. The authors call this the post-comprehension regime. Their proposed framework, Critique-Resilient Benchmarking, compares models through challenges and criticism while keeping humans responsible for final judgments.

An answer counts as correct within the framework when no adversary has convincingly demonstrated that it is wrong. Humans evaluate localized claims, allowing them to adjudicate disputes without fully understanding an entire solution. This operational definition makes the quality of both proposed answers and attempted critiques central to the evaluation process.

An itemized bipartite Bradley-Terry model jointly ranks systems for solving questions and generating difficult but solvable ones. In a mathematical evaluation involving eight frontier LLMs, the resulting scores are stable and correlate with external capability measures. These findings support adversarial evaluation as a way to obtain useful comparisons when comprehensive human assessment is difficult, with humans still deciding whether specific objections succeed.
icml-2026-benchmarking-at-the-edge-of-co.tldr: Critique-Resilient Benchmarking compares models through adversarial questions and critiques, using human judgments of localized claims when full solutions are hard to assess.

paragraphs: This paper examines how the representation of DNA affects genomic foundation models. Models that process raw nucleotide sequences may overlook regulatory context needed to interpret genetic differences. The authors propose incorporating that biological context directly into the input representation, so the model receives information about variation and annotations as part of its basic units of processing.

BioToken provides this tokenization framework, explicitly encoding variants and biological annotations. BioFM is a parameter-efficient model built around it. The approach places biological structure into the model’s inputs, making the representation itself a central design choice alongside model capacity. This is intended to help the system learn relationships relevant to genomic prediction.

On benchmarks including pathogenicity and expression prediction, BioFM outperforms the state-of-the-art models and specialized baselines described in the abstract, including Enformer. It also requires 100-fold less compute than current large-scale genomic models. The reported results support biologically informed representations as a route to stronger predictions and greater efficiency than scaling alone in the evaluated comparisons.
icml-2026-biotoken-and-biofm-biologicall.tldr: BioToken encodes biological context directly into genomic inputs, enabling BioFM to improve reported prediction results while using 100-fold less compute than large-scale genomic models.

paragraphs: Processing a long prompt before generating an answer can be expensive. Token-ranking methods try to reduce this prefill work by selecting the most relevant tokens, but ordinary task scores make it hard to judge the ranking itself. This paper introduces an answer-informed reference framework to study which prompt tokens contribute to answering a question.

One reference uses the model’s generated answer, while the other uses a human reference answer. With the latter, the authors find that as few as 10% of prompt tokens match full-context performance on LongBench across three evaluated models. Because this selection uses answer information, the result establishes the potential of effective token selection under that reference procedure.

The analysis also finds that existing rankings can deteriorate sharply at particular layers. CLAA addresses this instability by combining importance scores from consecutive layers, eliminating the observed accuracy collapse associated with choosing a single layer. A meaningful gap still separates the best heuristic from the ground-truth reference, indicating further room to improve token selection.
icml-2026-claa-cross-layer-attention-agg.tldr: CLAA stabilizes prompt-token selection by aggregating attention scores across layers, while answer-informed references reveal substantial remaining room for improvement.

paragraphs: Language models can deteriorate during long generations, repeating themselves or losing track of instructions. This paper formalizes that deterioration as cognitive fatigue, a generation-time state defined through measurable model signals. The term groups together changes in attention, internal representations, and uncertainty that could help detect declining performance while generation is still underway.

The proposed Fatigue Index combines reduced attention to the original prompt, representational drift, and entropy miscalibration. Its construction follows explicit requirements for monotonicity, boundedness, and interpretability. Across nine models with 1B–13B parameters, the index predicts task degradation with an AUROC of 0.95 and correlates with repetition at 0.94, supporting its use as a runtime diagnostic.

The findings also show that the behavior varies with model size and conditions. Instruction-tuned models below 3B collapse faster than base models, while the trend reverses at 7B. Longer contexts, evidence placed in the middle, and reduced numerical precision accelerate fatigue onset. These observations make the index useful for studying when reliability degrades, alongside monitoring the degradation itself.
icml-2026-cognitive-fatigue-in-autoregre.tldr: The Fatigue Index combines three internal signals to track and predict degradation during long language-model generations in the evaluated models.

paragraphs: Training can favor particular kinds of solutions even without an explicit penalty in the objective. This paper studies two such implicit preferences: smaller parameter norms and lower sharpness. Both have been used to explain why overparameterized networks generalize, and the authors investigate how their interaction changes the explanation.

Empirically, the learning rate controls a trade-off between these preferences. Small learning rates are associated with low parameter norm, while the Edge-of-Stability regime favors low sharpness. The results describe learning rate as a factor that changes the kind of solution training selects, making the relationship between optimization and generalization depend on competing effects.

The authors also prove a result for diagonal linear networks on a simple regression task: neither preference alone minimizes generalization error. This establishes the insufficiency of either explanation by itself in that setting. Together with the empirical observations, it motivates studying how norm and sharpness interact at non-negligible learning rates, rather than expecting one implicit regularization principle to explain the observed performance.
icml-2026-conflicting-biases-at-the-edge.tldr: The paper shows that learning rate mediates competing preferences for low norm and low sharpness, with neither alone optimizing generalization in its theoretical regression setting.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a model’s internal activity to influence its output. This paper finds that models can sometimes recover from steering that conflicts with their task, even while the intervention continues. The authors call this Endogenous Steering Resistance, or ESR, and investigate it using steering directions drawn from sparse autoencoder latents.

Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial resistance, while smaller Llama-3 and Gemma-2 models show it less frequently. The authors identify 26 latents that predict these episodes and describe them as off-topic detectors. Setting those latents to zero reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for internal mechanisms involved in checking consistency.

Resistance can also be strengthened. Self-monitoring prompts increase Llama-3.3-70B’s multi-attempt rate fivefold, and training on self-correction examples induces similar behavior in smaller models. The implications run in two directions: resistance could help protect models against adversarial manipulation, but it might also obstruct useful safety steering. Understanding these mechanisms therefore matters for both protection and controllability.
icml-2026-endogenous-resistance-to-activ.tldr: Some language models recover from task-conflicting activation steering, and the paper identifies internal signals and interventions associated with this resistance.

paragraphs: Geometric deep learning builds models that respect symmetries, while topological deep learning organizes computation around relationships among cells and local structures. This paper develops a mathematical framework connecting these approaches. Its order-equivariant neural networks, or OENNs, encompass standard graph message passing and sheaf neural networks within a shared construction.

The framework uses equivariant vector bundles over face posets or face categories to describe how information and transformations fit together. The authors characterize all linear maps that satisfy the required order-equivariance, then use that characterization to build network layers. This links the permitted computations directly to the structure the network is intended to respect.

They also prove universal approximation theorems for continuous order-equivariant maps, including new results for sheaf neural networks. These theorems establish representational capabilities for the specified class of functions. A further connection to category-equivariant networks extends the perspective from groups of symmetries to categories of transformations, giving graph and sheaf models a place within a broader account of equivariant learning.
icml-2026-foundations-of-equivariant-dee.tldr: Order-equivariant neural networks unify graph and sheaf architectures and provide new approximation guarantees within a broader mathematical treatment of symmetry.

paragraphs: Learning a stochastic system’s dynamics is difficult when observations are separated by large time gaps. Much of the motion between measurements is unseen. The paper addresses a gap between methods that require frequent measurements and geometric approaches whose arguments apply only to conservative systems, seeking to recover dynamics from sparse observations.

The authors reformulate inference as a stochastic control problem. Their method augments the observed data with likely intervening paths, using structure in the invariant density to guide that reconstruction. This density describes where the system tends to be found over time. Its geometry supplies information about plausible paths without requiring a specific parametric model of the underlying dynamics.

Applied to overdamped Langevin systems, the framework accurately recovers stochastic dynamics from severely undersampled data and outperforms existing methods on synthetic benchmarks. The findings show how geometric information can assist inference when temporal information is scarce. The paper presents this combination of trajectory reconstruction and geometric guidance as useful for stochastic system identification, with potential applications across physics, biology, and control.
icml-2026-from-geometry-to-dynamics-lear.tldr: A stochastic-control framework uses invariant-density geometry to reconstruct likely paths and recover Langevin dynamics from sparsely sampled observations.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers distribute computation among experts, making their statistical capacity depend on both the parameters active for an input and the possible routing decisions. This paper develops theory that separates those contributions. The distinction helps explain how a model’s total size relates to the computation and capacity actually used for each example.

The analysis first fixes routing patterns and then combines bounds across those patterns. The resulting measure of model complexity scales with active parameters and includes an additional routing cost. Under a manifold model of the data and smooth target functions, an analysis of squared-loss training yields a generalization bound with an approximation–estimation trade-off resembling that of dense networks.

A constructive approximation theorem shows that error can decrease by increasing active capacity or adding experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck in the construction. The authors derive scaling laws for model size, data, and compute-optimal choices. These results provide a worst-case statistical reference for separating theoretically certified behavior from effects attributable to routing structure or optimization.
icml-2026-generalization-and-scaling-law.tldr: The paper derives MoE generalization and scaling results by separating active parameter capacity from the additional complexity of routing.

paragraphs: An overparameterized model can fit its training data even when classification labels are random. Consequently, a small training error alone may say little about performance on new examples. This paper studies how to obtain informative error bounds for the Gibbs algorithm in this interpolation regime, using information that depends on the observed data.

The central result links behavior at different temperatures. Small training errors in the noisier, high-temperature regime already signal generalization in the low-temperature regime. This supplies information beyond the ability to fit data under low noise. The bounds also remain stable when the Gibbs algorithm is approximated using Langevin Monte Carlo, connecting the analysis to an implementable sampling procedure.

The theory motivates an algorithm for computing bounds. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN, these give nontrivial predictions close to test error for correctly labeled data, while retaining valid upper bounds for random labels. The significance is their ability to remain informative on learnable data while accounting for the contrasting behavior of models trained on meaningless labels.
icml-2026-generalization-of-gibbs-and-la.tldr: Data-dependent Gibbs error bounds use high-temperature training behavior to assess low-temperature generalization and remain stable under Langevin Monte Carlo approximation.

paragraphs: A goal-conditioned agent can learn from an experience in relation to goals beyond the one it was pursuing. Restricting each trajectory to a single goal leaves much of that information unused. All-goals learning addresses this by learning from each transition with respect to every goal, but repeatedly relabeling experiences can make the computation impractical.

Learning Everything all at Once, or LEO, changes how the network produces its outputs. It jointly predicts values and actions for every goal, enabling parallel updates through a single network pass. This makes the organization of computation central to the method: the agent can use an experience across goals without performing the naive relabeling procedure separately for each one.

LEO significantly outperforms the compared methods on goal-conditioned Craftax and is competitive with existing baselines in continuous control. It also achieves a reported 250-fold speedup over all-goals relabeling. These results support the approach as a practical way to extract more learning information from trajectories, with different performance outcomes across the evaluated environments.
icml-2026-goal-conditioned-agents-that-l.tldr: LEO learns about every goal in one network pass, achieving a 250-fold speedup over all-goals relabeling and strong results in the evaluated environments.

paragraphs: Encoder-only language models support tasks such as classification and retrieval, but multilingual encoders have received comparatively limited recent development. This paper introduces mmBERT, pretrained on three trillion tokens covering more than 1,800 languages. Its contribution includes both a multilingual model and a training strategy for making effective use of unevenly available language data.

The strategy combines phased data curation with scheduled language inclusion. More than 1,700 low-resource languages enter the training mixture only during the decay phase. The authors report that this timing substantially improves performance while obtaining more value from limited data without excessive repetition. Thus, when a language enters training is an important part of the approach.

The model also incorporates recent architectural and training advances to improve speed and multilingual coverage. Evaluations show significant gains over the previous generation across multiple tasks for both high-resource and low-resource languages. Released weights, data, and code accompany the model. The findings highlight training schedules as a useful tool for extending language coverage while improving performance.
icml-2026-mmbert-a-modern-multilingual-e.tldr: mmBERT improves multilingual encoder performance using phased training that introduces over 1,700 low-resource languages during the decay phase.

paragraphs: Directional antennas can support high throughput in mobile ad hoc networks, but their link choices must work together across the network. Decisions must account for interference, connectivity, antenna sectors, and half-duplex operation. NetDiff generates directional connection topologies together with a two-slot transmit/receive parity, treating these coupled decisions as a graph generation problem.

The model uses node-conditioned denoising diffusion. To improve global consistency, it adds Absolute Cross-Attentive Modulation tokens that supply network-wide signals independent of node ordering. These signals help the generated graph match overall quantities such as density and sector usage, bringing aggregate network requirements into a process that must also decide individual connections.

For changing node positions, partial diffusion updates an existing topology using only a few denoising steps. The reported results reach more than 95% of target performance with constant inference time. NetDiff outperforms heuristic and omnidirectional baselines and improves key metrics over a strong diffusion graph-transformer baseline, supporting both its global coordination mechanism and its use for rapid reconfiguration.
icml-2026-netdiff-graph-diffusion-with-i.tldr: NetDiff uses globally informed graph diffusion and partial updates to generate and rapidly reconfigure directional mobile-network topologies.

paragraphs: Verifying properties such as robustness or fairness in an ensemble of decision trees is computationally difficult, and many methods are tailored to one particular property. This paper introduces a shared perspective based on OC-space: the collection of possible combinations of predictions from the ensemble’s individual trees. It uses this representation to organize multiple verification problems.

The authors show that a wide range of existing tasks become searches through OC-space. Once expressed this way, the tasks can be answered in time linear or quadratic in the number of output configurations. Spatial index structures can further accelerate those searches, allowing different verification questions to benefit from a common computational approach.

The important qualification is that OC-space itself can grow exponentially with ensemble size. The approach therefore does not remove the underlying worst-case difficulty. Nevertheless, the authors find that enumerating all configurations is often feasible in practice, and their generic method can outperform methods designed for individual tasks. This makes the size of the configuration space practically consequential.
icml-2026-oc-space-a-unifying-perspectiv.tldr: OC-space expresses diverse tree-ensemble verification tasks as searches over output configurations, offering practical speedups despite potentially exponential space size.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations use networks to represent signals, and plain multilayer perceptrons are widely viewed as poor at learning high-frequency detail. That view has encouraged changes such as coordinate embeddings and specialized activations. This paper challenges the architectural explanation, arguing that degradation of stable rank during training helps explain the observed preference for low frequencies.

The authors empirically show that regulating network rank improves the fidelity of learned signals, including those represented by simple MLPs. Their experiments examine optimizers such as Muon, whose updates have high rank and are nearly orthogonal. This shifts attention toward the geometry of parameter updates as a way to improve what an existing architecture learns.

The improvements extend beyond simple ReLU networks to other implicit representation architectures. Across natural images, medical images, and novel view synthesis, the reported gains reach up to nine decibels of PSNR relative to the same architecture. These results support optimization and rank preservation as important contributors to high-frequency reconstruction quality, alongside the architectural choices that have traditionally received attention.
icml-2026-optimizing-rank-for-high-fidel.tldr: Rank-preserving optimization improves implicit neural representations, supporting the view that training dynamics contribute to plain MLPs’ difficulty with high-frequency detail.

paragraphs: Stem retrieval asks which missing musical component belongs with a given audio submix. The paper argues that discarding temporal information limits existing approaches to this task. PHALAR addresses that problem through a contrastive learning framework designed to preserve musically relevant relationships in its audio representations.

Its design combines a learned spectral pooling layer with a complex-valued output head. Together, these impose pitch-invariant and phase-equivariant biases: the representation is designed to handle pitch changes consistently while retaining structured responses to phase changes. This gives the model explicit guidance about which changes to treat as irrelevant and which temporal relationships to preserve.

PHALAR establishes new retrieval results across MoisesDB, Slakh, and ChocoChorales, with relative accuracy gains of up to approximately 70%, fewer than half the parameters, and sevenfold faster training. Its scores correlate more strongly with human coherence judgments than semantic baselines. Zero-shot beat tracking and linear chord probing further support the finding that the representations capture musical structure useful beyond the retrieval objective.
icml-2026-phalar-phasors-for-learned-mus.tldr: PHALAR uses structured musical audio representations to improve stem retrieval accuracy and efficiency while capturing information useful for beats and chords.

paragraphs: Tool-using language-model agents can execute code and interact with files and networks, making the security of their execution environments important. Containers are commonly used to isolate these activities. This paper introduces SandboxEscapeBench, an open benchmark for measuring whether an adversarial agent can escape such an environment under controlled evaluation conditions.

The benchmark assumes a motivated agent with shell access inside a container. Implemented as an Inspect AI capture-the-flag evaluation, it uses nested sandboxes, with the outer layer containing the flag and having no known vulnerabilities. The tested mechanisms span configuration errors, inappropriate privileges, kernel flaws, and weaknesses in runtime or orchestration systems.

The authors find that LLMs can identify and exploit vulnerabilities when those vulnerabilities are introduced. This finding concerns the vulnerable configurations evaluated and establishes a concrete capability relevant to containment. The benchmark supplies a way to test that capability as models improve, helping assess whether sandbox implementations continue to provide the isolation expected when deploying increasingly capable autonomous agents.
icml-2026-quantifying-frontier-llm-capab.tldr: SandboxEscapeBench measures container-escape capabilities in controlled environments and finds that LLMs can exploit deliberately introduced vulnerabilities.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a controlled task for studying how networks learn structured computation. A network receives a sequence of finite-group elements represented as real vectors and predicts their cumulative product. The operation can depend on order and cannot be learned by a linear model, making it useful for examining the roles of structure, encoding, and sequence length.

For two-layer networks trained from vanishing initialization, the authors prove that learning proceeds through one irreducible group representation at a time. The order depends on Fourier statistics of the input encoding. They also show that perfect learning by these networks requires hidden width exponential in sequence length, exposing a substantial scaling cost in this shallow setting.

Deeper constructions exploit associativity, which allows products to be grouped without changing the result. A recurrent network can combine elements sequentially in k steps, while a multilayer network combines neighboring pairs in parallel using logarithmically many layers. These constructions show how architecture can exploit the task’s algebraic structure to improve scaling and illuminate the mechanics of learning.
icml-2026-sequential-group-composition-a.tldr: Sequential group composition reveals how encoding shapes shallow-network learning and how architectures exploiting associativity can greatly improve sequence-length scaling.

paragraphs: This paper develops confidence bounds for the variance of bounded random variables. Its empirical Bernstein inequalities use observed data to quantify uncertainty about variance. The guarantees require constant conditional mean and variance, but do not additionally require independent or identically distributed observations, making the results relevant to sequential decision settings.

The authors provide versions for fixed sample sizes and for sequential sampling that ends at a stopping time. In the independent, identically distributed case, the bounds are asymptotically sharp: their leading term matches an oracle Bernstein bound that knows the mean and the variance of squared deviations from that mean. This identifies precisely the sense in which the bounds adapt optimally.

Compared with a widely used variance inequality based on self-bounding random variables, the new results offer both theoretical improvements and better empirical performance. The methods also extend to any separable Hilbert space. Together, these contributions strengthen variance uncertainty estimates while accommodating the stated forms of dependence and data-dependent stopping.
icml-2026-sharp-empirical-bernstein-ineq.tldr: New variance confidence bounds allow sequential sampling under constant conditional moments and asymptotically match an oracle’s leading term for iid data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how adversarial image–text inputs cause vision-language models to produce toxic outputs. Existing approaches often assess toxicity only after image generation finishes, obscuring when harmful content develops. STARE instead examines the intermediate denoising trajectory, treating the sequence of image-generation steps as a source of information about vulnerabilities.

The framework combines a high-level prompt editor with low-level text-to-image fine-tuning through Group Relative Policy Optimization. The authors report a 68% improvement in attack success rate over the compared state-of-the-art black-box and white-box baselines. This establishes the effectiveness of jointly optimizing prompts and the image-generation process in their evaluation.

The analysis also identifies a temporal pattern induced by optimization. Conceptual harms become concentrated in early semantic stages, while harms involving details concentrate in later refinement stages; unoptimized models show more diffuse toxicity. The authors call this Optimization-Induced Phase Alignment. It suggests predictable windows for examining toxicity formation and provides a diagnostic basis for safety mechanisms that account for different generation phases.
icml-2026-stare-step-wise-temporal-align.tldr: STARE improves multimodal red-teaming and finds that adversarial optimization concentrates different kinds of harmful content into distinct image-generation phases.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents can make effective decisions while offering little insight into how those decisions arise. This paper introduces ProtoSAC, which builds an inspectable decision process into Soft Actor-Critic. It targets continuous action spaces, where approaches based on explaining or copying a pretrained black-box agent have faced limitations.

ProtoSAC learns prototypes representing interpretable clusters of states. Each prototype has an associated Gaussian action distribution. For a new state, the actor generates actions through a mixture weighted by similarity to these prototypes. A decision can therefore be examined through the states it resembles and the contributions of their associated action distributions.

This structure makes interpretability part of the actor’s computation and allows its decisions to be decomposed into prototype contributions. In the evaluated continuous-control environments, ProtoSAC matches standard SAC performance while improving interpretability. The result supports prototype-based action generation as a way to expose the basis of continuous decisions without the performance loss that might otherwise make such an architecture difficult to adopt.
icml-2026-this-state-looks-like-that-sel.tldr: ProtoSAC makes continuous-control decisions inspectable through learned state prototypes while matching standard SAC performance in the tested environments.

paragraphs: Walrus is a transformer foundation model developed primarily for fluid-like continuum dynamics. Building such a model requires learning across heterogeneous physical data while maintaining stable predictions over time. Differences in spatial resolution and dimensionality also complicate efficient training, so the paper addresses computational organization alongside the forecasting problem.

The authors introduce stabilization based on harmonic analysis, load-balanced distributed training across two- and three-dimensional data, and tokenization that adapts to compute. Walrus is pretrained on nineteen scenarios spanning astrophysics, geoscience, rheology, plasma physics, acoustics, and classical fluids. These methods support learning from varied dynamics within a shared model.

Experiments show better short-term and long-term predictions than prior foundation models on downstream tasks and across the pretraining data. Ablations support the contributions of the proposed techniques to forecast stability, training throughput, and transfer performance. The findings connect improvements in numerical behavior and training efficiency to the broader objective of a reusable model for diverse continuum systems, particularly those with fluid-like dynamics.
icml-2026-walrus-a-cross-domain-foundati.tldr: Walrus combines stabilized forecasting and efficient heterogeneous training to improve continuum-dynamics predictions across diverse physical scenarios.
